fixes.explanation: Kill. That's the word the text uses: Ishbi-benob resolved to kill David. I think a worn-out king is the last person who should be on that man's list. The text says David became exhausted just before this.
That's the oath. David's men swear, "You must never again go out with us to battle…" It's a firm line, and I bet it came out of a very tense moment. They swear it, and that tells me they mean it.

It's actually False. The text says this man of great stature at Gath had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. Armor isn't mentioned at all. So the unusual thing the text points out is his fingers and toes, not anything he wore.

False, and good catch. The text never mentions bronze armor on this man. It says he had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. That's the detail the text gives about him.

That's him. When the man at Gath taunts Israel, Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei kills him. So this Jonathan is David's nephew. A taunt is a risky thing to say to Israel, and here it's the last thing that man says.

Absalom was David's son by Maacah, daughter of King Talmai of Geshur (2 Samuel 3:3). He's famous, so his name comes to mind fast. But here the text says Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei kills the man. Absalom isn't named in this scene.

Five is one too many. The text counts them up as "…these four descendants of Rapha in Gath…" Those are Ishbi-benob, Saph, the brother of Goliath the Gittite and the man with six fingers on each hand. The text names two of them and describes the other two, and then gives the tally of four.
